pages.x: In 1958 Mao Zedong launched a campaign to overtake Britain's industry within fifteen years. Peasants were herded into huge people's communes, where they ate in shared dining halls and gave up their land, their tools and even their cooking pots.

Across the country millions built little backyard furnaces to make steel, feeding them pots, pans, door hinges and tools and burning whole forests for fuel. Most of what came out was useless lumps of iron. Meanwhile crops rotted in the fields, because the farmers were busy at the furnaces.

Sparrows ate grain, so Mao declared them pests. People banged pots and drums day and night so that the birds could not land, until they dropped dead from exhaustion. With the sparrows gone, locusts and other insects multiplied and ate even more of the crops.

Local officials, afraid to look disloyal, reported impossible harvests, and the state took grain on the strength of their boasts, leaving villages with nothing. When Marshal Peng Dehuai wrote to Mao in 1959 about the hunger, he was purged, and after that no one dared to speak.
From 1959 to 1961 the countryside starved. People ate tree bark, grass and clay. Officials beat or killed farmers caught hiding food, and all the while China went on selling grain abroad.

In 1961 the leaders quietly ended the campaign. Liu Shaoqi, the head of state, told a party meeting in 1962 that the disaster was three parts nature and seven parts man-made. Mao stepped back from daily power, but he never forgave his critics, and four years later he turned on them.

The Great Leap Forward caused the deadliest famine in history. For decades it was barely spoken of in China, where it is called the three years of difficulty and blamed largely on bad weather. Its memory helped convince later leaders to give the land back to farming families.
